reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Timber Pile Accessories
sections.summary: Timber pile toe protection: steel boots (cover full toe without trimming) or steel points (require toe trimming). Head protection: heavy metal banding required when Rndr > 200 kips (AASHTO 2010). Splices not recommended for timber piles — virtually impossible to develop full bending strength. Longer piles should be ordered rather than splicing.
sections.body:
Potential problems during timber pile driving include splitting and brooming at pile toe and head, splitting or bowing of the pile body, and pile breakage during driving. Protective attachments at toe and head minimize these problems.

Pile Toe Attachments (Section 16.1.1): Steel boots cover the entire pile toe without trimming. Steel points require trimming the toe to fit. Both are secured quickly in the field by placing the device over the pile toe, nailing shoe straps, and anchoring.

Attachments at Pile Head (Section 16.1.2): American Wood Preservers Institute (Collin 2012) recommends banding timber piles with heavy metal strapping at the pile head prior to driving to prevent splitting. AASHTO (2010) requires collars, bands, or other anti-splitting devices when Rndr > 200 kips.

Splices (Section 16.1.3): Timber pile splices are undesirable. It is virtually impossible to develop full bending strength of a spliced timber pile. AASHTO (2010) prohibits timber pile splices unless specified in the contract documents or directed in writing by the engineer. When lengths prove insufficient, longer piles should be ordered or the foundation redesigned with additional piles.
key_points: Steel boots: full toe coverage, no trimming; steel points: require toe trimming
Head banding with heavy metal strapping recommended by AWPI; required by AASHTO when Rndr > 200 kips
Timber pile splices not recommended — impossible to develop full bending strength
AASHTO: timber piles shall not be spliced unless specified in contract documents or engineer directive
Preferred solution for insufficient pile length: order longer piles or redesign with additional piles
sections.applicability: Toe protection, head banding, and splicing guidance for timber pile installation — emphasis on avoiding splices.

sections.title: Steel H-Pile Accessories
sections.summary: H-pile shoes recommended through dense gravels, boulders, fills, and to sloping rock; manufactured from cast steel ASTM A148/A148M Grade 90-60; attached with fillet welds (5/16 inch minimum) along exterior flanges. Pile toe plate reinforcement (welded plates to flanges/web) not recommended. H-pile splices: full penetration groove weld along web and both flanges, or commercially manufactured H-pile splicer. Full penetration welds required when full bending strength is needed.
sections.body:
Pile Toe Attachments (Section 16.2.1): H-piles are generally easy to install but may develop toe damage through man-made fills, very dense gravel, or boulders. Damage includes deformation and separation of flanges and web. Commercially manufactured pile shoes minimize or prevent toe damage. Shoes also help distribute high localized contact stresses on rock, particularly on sloping rock surfaces.

H-pile shoes manufactured to ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60) cast steel. Attached with fillet welds along the outside of each flange — lower flanges beveled, 5/16 inch fillet weld (or greater depending on flange thickness). Multiple styles/shapes available — for a given set of conditions, shoes from different manufacturers are considered equivalent if manufactured from similar strength materials and fabrication techniques. Minor configuration differences given minimum importance unless a specific shape offers a definite advantage.

Note: pile toe reinforcement consisting of steel plates welded to flanges and web is NOT recommended — does not provide protection or increased strength at the critical flange-to-web connection.

Splices (Section 16.2.2): Full penetration groove weld along web and both flanges (preferred). Commercially manufactured H-pile splicers also used. Some agencies use a welded square or diamond backer plate detail with welded splice. H-pile splices must satisfy all structural resistance requirements for axial compression, tension, and bending under foundation loading. Full penetration weld preferred when full bending strength is required. H-pile splicers can be used for lower load conditions.
key_points: H-pile shoes: cast steel ASTM A148/A148M Grade 90-60; attached with beveled fillet welds (5/16 inch min.) along exterior flanges
Shoe styles are considered equivalent across manufacturers if same material/fabrication — shape matters only for specific subsurface conditions
Welded plate toe reinforcement on flanges/web NOT recommended — no protection or strength at critical flange-web connection
H-pile splice: full penetration groove weld on web and both flanges — preferred when full bending strength required
H-pile splicer: alternative for lower load cases; must satisfy axial, tension, and bending strength requirements
sections.applicability: Pile shoe specifications and splice details for steel H-piles driven through obstructions, dense materials, or to rock.

sections.title: Steel Pipe Pile Accessories
sections.summary: Closed-end pipe: flat closure plate (0.75-1.0 inch thick for OD ≤18 inch, 5/8 inch oversize with 5/16 inch fillet weld) or conical toe attachment (cast steel A148 Grade 90-60; rock crusher preferred for sloping bedrock). Open-end pipe: inside or outside flange cutting shoes (A148 Grade 90-60) through dense gravel or rock. Pipe splices: full penetration groove weld with backing ring (preferred when full bending strength needed) or friction drive-fit splicer. Constrictor plates used inside large-diameter open-end pipe (≥36 inch) to force plugged behavior.
sections.body:
Pile Toe Attachments (Section 16.3.1): Closed-end pipe piles most frequently use a flat closure plate welded at pile toe. Plate thickness: 0.75-1.0 inch for OD ≤18 inch; thicker plates may be required for larger diameters. Closure plate diameter: typically 5/8 inch larger than pile OD (for 5/16 inch fillet weld) or same OD with beveled partial penetration weld. Plate material: ASTM A36/A36M or better.

Conical toe attachments (rounded or 60-degree point): cost more than flat plates; flat plates generally develop higher unit toe resistance. Conical attachments: full or partial penetration groove weld; ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60) cast steel.

Rock crusher driving shoe: preferred for sloping bedrock; thick flat plate with heavy steel plates forming a 45-degree point.

Open-end pipe in dense gravel or to rock: cutting shoes protect against deformation and distribute contact stresses. Inside flange and outside flange types available. Outside flange increases perimeter diameter and can reduce shaft resistance. Both types from ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60) cast steel.

Large diameter open-end pipe (≥36 inch): thicker wall toe section can function as inside cutting shoe with same OD as design pile — distributes stresses, reduces damage on boulders, sloping rock, or batter installations.

Splices (Section 16.3.2): Full penetration groove welds with backing ring (preferred when full bending strength required). Backing ring: aids alignment, has pins to maintain gap for root pass. Friction drive-fit splicers: cast ASTM A27 (Grade 65-35) or A148/A148M (Grade 90-60); tapered frictional connection; 3/8 inch bearing at midpoint for load transfer. Friction splicers must be fully seated before fillet weld if full bending strength required; otherwise welding after seating may crack. Fillet welds to top and bottom pile sections required for full bending strength.

Constrictor Plates (Section 16.3.3): Welded inside large-diameter open-end pipe piles to force plugged behavior at a targeted depth. Used to increase nominal resistance by engaging larger toe area. Research on LDOEP with constrictor plates ongoing.
key_points: Closure plate: 0.75-1.0 inch thick for OD ≤18 inch; 5/8 inch oversize + 5/16 inch fillet weld; ASTM A36 or better
Conical toe (A148 Gr.90-60): rounded or 60-degree point; flat plates give higher unit toe resistance; rock crusher preferred on sloping bedrock
Cutting shoes for open-end pipe: inside or outside flange, A148 Gr.90-60; outside flange may reduce shaft resistance
Full penetration weld with backing ring: preferred for full bending strength; friction splicer (A27 or A148) for lower load cases
Friction splicer: must be fully seated before fillet weld to avoid cracking; fillet welds required for full bending strength
Constrictor plates (≥36 inch OD): welded inside pile to force plugged behavior and increase toe resistance
sections.applicability: Toe protection and splicing for closed-end and open-end steel pipe piles, including material specifications, welding details, and constrictor plate use in large-diameter open-end piles.

sections.title: Precast Concrete Pile Accessories
sections.summary: Concrete pile toe attachments not routinely used except in hard driving/rock conditions: flat cast steel shoe or Oslo/Rock Injector Point (3.5-inch hardened steel point; chisels into most rock types) — must be cast in, not field-attached. Embedded H-pile or pipe toe sections used where penetration depth is difficult. Splices: seven types evaluated (Table 16-1) — epoxy dowel, Kie-Lock mechanical, ICP welded, NU Chuck bolted, UF Tube grouted, GYA mechanical, Macalloy post-tensioned. Avoid splices whenever possible — prestress ends are not effectively prestressed due to development length.
sections.body:
Pile Toe Attachments (Section 16.4.1): Concrete pile toes may be damaged in compression under hard driving. For hard driving conditions and toe bearing on rock, cast steel toe attachments are added during casting — not field-installed.

Flat cast steel shoe: provides compression resistance. Oslo Point / Rock Injector Point: 3.5-inch diameter hardened steel point in steel casting; chisels into most rock types to ensure proper seating. All toe attachments must be cast into the pile — field attachment not possible.

Embedded H-pile or pipe section: not for toe protection but to facilitate penetration through very dense or hard materials. Section must be appropriately sized for concrete section, foundation loading, and subsurface conditions.

Splices (Section 16.4.2): All prestressed concrete piles driven in the U.S. are prestressed. Pile ends are not effectively prestressed due to development length — special precautions required when splicing. Avoid splicing whenever possible by ordering sufficient pile lengths.

Table 16-1 (after Mullins and Sen 2015) summarizes seven splice types on capacity, failure type, durability, installation difficulty, and U.S. production:
- Epoxy Dowel: poor capacity; ductile failure; good durability; moderate/poor installation; U.S. produced
- Kie-Lock Mechanical: good capacity; ductile failure; moderate durability; good installation; not U.S. produced
- ICP Welded: good capacity; brittle failure; moderate durability; moderate installation; not U.S. produced
- NU Chuck Bolted: good capacity; brittle failure; moderate durability; untested installation; U.S. produced
- UF Tube Grouted: good capacity; ductile failure; good durability; poor installation; U.S. produced (voided piles)
- GYA Mechanical: good capacity; ductile failure; moderate durability; good installation; not U.S. produced
- Macalloy Post-Tensioned: good capacity; ductile failure; good durability; moderate/poor installation; not U.S. produced

Epoxy dowel splice: holes cast or drilled in lower section; dowels protruding from top section; sheet metal form placed; epoxy poured; driving can resume 1-2 days after epoxy placement. Comparatively inexpensive but time consuming.
key_points: Oslo/Rock Injector Point: 3.5-inch hardened steel point cast into pile; chisels into rock for proper seating
All concrete pile toe attachments must be cast-in — no field attachment
Avoid splicing concrete piles — pile ends not effectively prestressed due to development length
Table 16-1: seven concrete pile splice types — only Kie-Lock, GYA, and Macalloy provide good capacity with ductile failure
ICP and NU Chuck: brittle failure mode — not preferred
Epoxy dowel splice: 1-2 day cure time before driving resumes; holes cast or field-drilled
UF Tube splice: voided piles only
Foreign-made splices (Kie-Lock, ICP, GYA, Macalloy) require special exceptions on federally funded projects

tables.description: Summary of precast concrete pile splices (after Mullins and Sen 2015) — name, type, capacity rating, failure type (ductile/brittle), durability, installation difficulty, and U.S. produced status for epoxy dowel, Kie-Lock, ICP, NU Chuck, UF Tube, GYA, and Macalloy splices

sections.applicability: Toe attachments and splice options for precast prestressed concrete piles, including Oslo/rock points, embedded steel toe sections, and comparative evaluation of seven concrete pile splice systems.

sections.title: Welded Splices and Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Field weld quality is critical — weld failure during driving most commonly traced to poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, or non-compliance with approved procedures. Temperature requirements: preheat to 70°F within 3 inches of weld before welding; maintain ≥50°F during welding; no welding below 0°F ambient. H-pile full penetration weld: 45-degree bevel with 1/8 or 1/4 inch root opening. Driving shoes attached with partial penetration groove weld along full flange length (not spot welds).
sections.body:
Field welding is required for many pile splices and toe attachments. Weld quality directly determines pile structural resistance. Michigan DOT 'Field Manual for Pile Welding' (2012) and NYSDOT 'Pile Driving Inspection Manual' (2012) provide detailed guidance, including minimum splice times as a function of pile section and splice type.

Common weld failure causes: poor pile surface preparation; insufficient bevel or root opening; non-compliance with approved welding procedures or splice details. Bending stresses during hammer-pile misalignment can crack pipe pile welds. Low-temperature welding without preheating can crack H-pile splices immediately after driving resumes.

Welding Surface Preparation (Section 16.5.1): Joint area must be cleaned before welding. Bevels must be correct for full penetration — without appropriate bevel, weld penetration is reduced and full penetration groove weld is impossible. H-pile: typically 45-degree bevel with 1/8 or 1/4 inch root opening for full penetration weld. Section alignment and root opening must be verified before welding when H-pile splicers are used.

Temperature Requirements (Section 16.5.2): When ambient temperature is below 32°F, preheat steel to minimum 70°F within 3 inches of the weld immediately prior to welding. Maintain minimum 50°F until welding is complete. No welding below 0°F ambient.

Welding Pile Toe Accessories (Section 16.5.3): Toe attachments on H-piles and pipe piles must be welded following approved procedures by approved welders. Spot welds (one web + one flange corner) are insufficient — can result in loss of driving shoe during hard driving. Partial penetration groove weld along full length of H-pile flange greatly reduces risk of shoe loss or poor performance.
key_points: Weld failures traced to: poor surface prep, insufficient bevel/root opening, non-compliance with procedures
H-pile weld: 45-degree bevel + 1/8 or 1/4 inch root opening required for full penetration
Pipe pile: verify section alignment and root opening before welding when using H-pile splicers
Temperature: preheat to 70°F within 3 inches; maintain ≥50°F during welding; no welding below 0°F
Toe shoe attachment: partial penetration groove weld along full flange length — spot welds insufficient (shoe loss risk)
Key references: Michigan DOT Field Manual for Pile Welding (2012); NYSDOT Pile Driving Inspection Manual (2012)
sections.applicability: Field welding requirements for pile splices and toe attachments, including surface preparation, temperature constraints, bevel requirements, and minimum weld details to prevent splice failure during driving.
